text: Authenticated encryption should protect both confidentiality and integrity. Bind associated data consistently, reject altered authentication tags, and follow the mode's IV requirements for every encryption under a key.
For GCM, IV generation must satisfy the uniqueness requirement for each key across messages and execution contexts. A local two-call difference alone does not establish a sound nonce lifecycle.
Manage cryptographic keys across generation, distribution, storage, rotation, and destruction. Protect key material wherever it is processed or stored.
Generate security-sensitive keys, IVs, tokens, and reset values with a cryptographically secure random source. Ordinary pseudorandom generators are intended for non-security uses.
Password-based key derivation for storage depends on a specified derivation function, salt, and iteration count. Treat salt and work-factor validation as part of the security contract.

Store passwords using an adaptive password-hashing construction with an individual salt and calibrated work factor. Fast general-purpose hashes and plaintext storage do not provide the intended resistance to offline guessing.
CMS block padding adds N trailing octets each with value N, including a full block when the input length is already a multiple of the block size. This makes the padding unambiguous to remove.

A comparison used for authentication can disclose secret information through observable timing differences. Use a comparison primitive designed for authentication instead of an early-exit string comparison.

source: OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: In a typical TLS connection, a server certificate lets the client verify the server's identity while establishing an encrypted connection.
Parsing a certificate is not enough to trust it. Validate the certificate chain, trust anchor, time and intended identity under the application policy before accepting the peer.
Keep access tokens, encryption keys, passwords, and other primary secrets out of application logs and diagnostics. Review both normal and error paths for unintended disclosure.
A predictable initialization vector in CBC mode can expose encrypted data to pattern and dictionary attacks. Follow the selected mode's IV-generation requirement rather than using a fixed value.

source: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: Prepared statements with parameterized queries keep SQL code separate from supplied data values. Bind untrusted values through parameters rather than constructing SQL text with them.

source: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: Encode untrusted values for the exact HTML, attribute, JavaScript, URL, or CSS output context in which they appear. Preserve benign content while preventing the browser from interpreting it as active code.
Path traversal can make a pathname built from external input resolve outside an intended parent directory. Neutralize special path elements so the operation stays within that directory.

source: OWASP Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: Constrain server-side requests to approved destinations and schemes. Validate domain and resolved address behavior, including redirects, while retaining legitimate allowed requests.

source: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/OS_Command_Injection_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: Prefer a language library to a shell command. If a command is necessary, keep the executable fixed and separate untrusted data into validated arguments rather than constructing a shell string.
Perform server-side authorization for each requested resource and operation using trusted identity and policy data. A hard-to-guess object identifier is not a substitute for an access decision.
Session identifiers need unpredictable generation and server-side lifecycle checks. Validate, rotate, expire, and invalidate sessions according to the application's authentication policy.

source: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: State-changing authenticated requests need a server-side anti-CSRF control such as a validated session-bound token. Reject missing or mismatched tokens while allowing legitimate requests.
Transaction authorization should be enforced server-side, and each operation should use unique authorization credentials to prevent replay of credentials across operations.
An idempotency key lets a server recognize a retried request. Repeating a request with the same key avoids performing the same operation twice.
